planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; set stock well back from walkways since it suckers and spreads over time.

directions: Kirilow's false spirea is a vigorous, thicket-forming shrub related to the more common Sorbaria sorbifolia, but it grows considerably larger and coarser, making it better suited to screening or naturalizing on slopes than to small borders. Large pinnate leaves give the plant a fern-like texture, and in mid to late summer it sends up tall, dense panicles of small creamy white flowers that attract a range of pollinators. Because it spreads by root suckers, give it room to colonize or plan to divide and remove unwanted shoots annually; cutting the oldest canes to the ground in late winter keeps the colony looking fresh. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and some drought once established, but flowers and foliage look best with consistent moisture.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery divisions in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants resent wet, heavy clay.

directions: Fuji Blue forms a tidy, long-lived clump of narrow, needle-like foliage topped from midsummer into fall with two-lipped, violet-blue tubular flowers typical of the mint family. It is one of the more compact and garden-adaptable dragonheads, performing best in a sunny rock garden, scree bed, or crevice planting where drainage is sharp. Deadheading spent flower spikes encourages a longer repeat bloom, and the clump rarely needs division except to propagate more plants. Once established, it tolerates considerable summer drought and does not require staking despite its airy appearance.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring into moist, humus-rich, peaty soil in light shade; a cool, sheltered peat bed or shaded rock garden wall suits it best.

directions: Loch Ewe is a hybrid between the white-flowered New Zealand species Ourisia macrophylla and the red-flowered South American Ourisia coccinea, combining the parents' vigor with warm orange-pink, tubular flowers held above neat rosettes of leathery evergreen leaves in late spring and early summer. It spreads gently by short rhizomes to form a well-mannered mat rather than running aggressively, making it suitable for peat beds, shaded walls, and woodland garden edges. Consistent moisture and cool root conditions are essential; it struggles in hot, dry summers and benefits from a humus-rich mulch. Named for the garden at Inverewe in Scotland where the cross was raised, it is a reliable choice for connoisseurs of shaded alpine and peat-garden plantings.

planting.note: Start seed in a well-draining cactus mix in warmth, or plant nursery-grown specimens in spring in full sun and extremely sharp drainage; protect young plants from frost and winter rain.

directions: One of the most distinctive plants of the Baja California peninsula, the boojum tree grows as a single tapering, carrot-shaped trunk studded with short twiggy side branches and topped by a tuft of small leaves, resembling an inverted root more than a conventional tree. Growth is extraordinarily slow, so plants kept in containers for many years will show little change in height while still being viable, long-lived specimens. It demands full sun, scorching heat, and soil that drains instantly after rain, since root rot in cool, wet conditions is the primary cause of failure in cultivation outside its native desert range. Mature plants in habitat eventually produce small, fragrant, creamy flowers in summer and can live for centuries, but this is a specimen plant for frost-free, arid gardens or large containers rather than typical landscaping.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; stake young trees loosely in windy sites until the root system establishes.

directions: Japanese blueberry tree forms a dense, oval-headed evergreen prized in warm-climate landscapes for year-round color interest: new leaves emerge with a coppery orange-red flush before maturing to glossy dark green, and older leaves scattered through the canopy turn red before dropping, so the tree never looks bare but always shows a bit of color. Small, fragrant white flowers in spring are followed by inconspicuous blue-black fruit that draws songbirds without creating significant litter. Growth is slow to moderate, and the tree takes well to shaping as a clipped screen, hedge, or street tree in addition to its natural rounded form. It prefers full sun and regular water while establishing, then tolerates considerable heat and moderate drought once mature, though it is not reliably cold-hardy outside zone 8.
